title: Amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day readmission after a heart failure hospitalization
text:
This report is written to be self-contained.

Section 2 is the Methods section, written in manuscript prose. It can be lifted into the paper with light editing for house style. Every analytic choice is stated together with the reason for it, so that a reviewer’s “why did you do it this way?” is already answered in the text.
Section 3 contains every table and figure, each with a caption and a note that states exactly what the numbers are and what they are not.
Section 4 is a pre-written Limitations section.
Section 5 anticipates the statistical criticisms this design attracts and gives the prepared answer to each.
Section 7 is the verification log: the checks that were run on this analysis and their outcome.

Numbers in the prose below are generated from the data at render time, not typed. If a number appears in the text it is the same number as in the corresponding table by construction.
Two conventions that matter for the write-up. First, the exposure is called amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder throughout and must be called that in the manuscript; see Section 2.4 for why “methamphetamine” is wrong. Second, absolute effects (risk differences) are the headline result and odds ratios are secondary, because 30-day readmission is common and an odds ratio overstates a risk ratio when the outcome is common.

title: Amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day readmission after a heart failure hospitalization
text:
2.1 Data source
Data came from the Healthcare Cost and Utilization Project (HCUP) Nationwide Readmissions Database (NRD) for calendar years 2016 through 2022, sponsored by the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality. The NRD is constructed from HCUP State Inpatient Databases containing verified patient linkage numbers and is designed to support national estimates of readmission for all payers and for the uninsured. It is the largest all-payer readmission database in the United States.
Three features of the NRD determine much of the design that follows.

Linkage is within calendar year only. The verified patient linkage number (NRD_VISITLINK) is re-issued each year, so a patient cannot be followed from December of one year into January of the next. This is why December discharges are excluded from the index cohort (Section 2.3).
The unit of observation is the discharge, not the patient. A patient may contribute more than one index admission within a year. This is addressed by sensitivity analysis S1 (Section 3.8).
The sampling design is a stratified cluster sample of hospitals. Discharge weights (DISCWT), hospital clusters (HOSP_NRD) and sampling strata (NRD_STRATUM) must be used for every estimate, including descriptive ones.

The NRD contains no geographic identifiers below the national level and no race or ethnicity variable. Neither can be adjusted for, and both are stated as limitations (Section 4) rather than left for a reviewer to discover. Because the study window is entirely within the ICD-10-CM/PCS era, no ICD-9-to-ICD-10 crosswalk was required and no transition artefact is present.

title: Amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day readmission after a heart failure hospitalization
text:
2.2 Study design and survey structure
This is a retrospective cohort study of index hospitalizations, using the complex survey design throughout.
The design object was constructed once, on the complete cohort, with survey::svydesign() using HOSP_YR as the cluster, STRATUM_YR as the stratum, DISCWT as the weight and nest = TRUE. Every subsequent analysis is a subset() of that single design object.
HOSP_NRD and NRD_STRATUM are re-used across data years and do not identify the same hospital or stratum in different years. Pooling years without making these identifiers year-unique collapses unrelated hospitals into a single cluster and produces standard errors that are too small. STRATUM_YR and HOSP_YR are therefore formed by concatenating the discharge year onto each identifier before the design is built. The presence of both is asserted at run time; the analysis stops rather than proceeding without them.
Filtering the data frame and then rebuilding a design on the filtered rows is not equivalent to subsetting the design: it discards strata that retain no observations and produces variance estimates that are wrong in a way no diagnostic reports. Every restriction in this analysis – the analytic cohort, each subgroup, each sensitivity analysis – is a subset() of the original design.
Strata containing a single primary sampling unit were centred at the grand mean (options(survey.lonely.psu = "adjust")) rather than dropped, which is the conservative option; the number of such strata is reported in Section 3.10. Confidence intervals constructed by hand use t critical values on the design degrees of freedom rather than 1.96.

title: Amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day readmission after a heart failure hospitalization
text:
2.3 Cohort construction
The index cohort comprises adult hospitalizations with a principal diagnosis of heart failure: ICD-10-CM I50.x, or hypertensive heart disease with heart failure (I11.0) or hypertensive heart and chronic kidney disease with heart failure (I13.0, I13.2); 26 codes, listed in Section 6. A principal-diagnosis definition was chosen over an any-listed definition because it identifies admissions for heart failure rather than admissions with heart failure, which is the population in which 30-day readmission is a policy-relevant endpoint. The hypertensive codes are required, not optional: from 1 October 2016 the ICD-10-CM guidelines presume a causal link between hypertension and heart failure and sequence I11.0/I13.x first, with I50 as a secondary code. An I50-only principal definition therefore loses most heart failure admissions from late 2016 onward, non-randomly. Heart failure phenotype is taken from any listed I50 subtype code for the same reason.
Exclusions were applied in the following order:

age under 18 years;
any non-stimulant substance use disorder without a stimulant code (Section 2.4), so that the comparator arm is clean;
short-term transfers out, because the discharge is not the end of the episode of care and a “readmission” would be an artefact of the transfer;
in-hospital deaths, which cannot be readmitted;
December discharges, which have less than 30 days of follow-up available within the linkage year.

Records excluded at steps 3 to 5 are retained in the cohort file and flagged, not deleted, so that in-hospital mortality can be described on the correct denominator before the survivor restriction is applied.

title: Amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day readmission after a heart failure hospitalization
text:
2.4 Exposure
The exposure is amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder, defined by any listed ICD-10-CM code in the F15 block (45 codes) on the index admission.
This exposure must not be described as “methamphetamine”. In ICD-10-CM, F15 is Other stimulant related disorders. It covers amphetamine-type stimulants including methamphetamine, but it also includes caffeine, and it excludes cocaine, which is coded separately in F14. Administrative data cannot separate methamphetamine from other agents within F15. Calling the exposure “methamphetamine-associated” would be a coding error visible to any reviewer who opens the code book, and would misstate what was measured. The correct phrase, used throughout, is amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder.
Two refinements were pre-specified:

Remission codes (F15.11, F15.21, F15.91) are excluded from the exposed arm. Remission is a clinically distinct state and including it would dilute the estimate toward the null. Those records are retained as a separate stratum and compared with the unexposed arm in sensitivity analysis S5b.
The comparator excludes any other substance use disorder (F10.1x/F10.2x alcohol abuse and dependence, F11 through F14, F16, F18, F19). A comparator containing patients with opioid or cocaine use disorder would not be a “no substance use disorder” group, and the contrast would be uninterpretable.

Assignment is three-way and order-dependent: a stimulant code is tested first, so a patient with polysubstance coding that includes F15 is classified as exposed. The question is about stimulant exposure, not stimulant-only exposure.

title: Amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day readmission after a heart failure hospitalization
text:
2.5 Outcome
The primary outcome is 30-day all-cause readmission, defined as the first non-elective inpatient admission occurring 1 to 30 days after discharge from the index admission, linked within the calendar year.
All-cause readmission was chosen, rather than heart-failure-specific readmission, because it is the endpoint used by the Hospital Readmissions Reduction Program and reported in the heart failure literature, and because cause-specific readmission requires an assumption about the coding of the readmission that all-cause readmission does not. Cause of readmission is reported descriptively (Section 3.6) rather than used as the primary endpoint. The trauma exclusion applied in some of this group’s earlier NRD studies was deliberately not carried over.
Where more than one candidate readmission fell on the same day, the record with the smallest KEY_NRD was selected, which makes the choice deterministic and reproducible; the number of ties broken is reported by the cohort build.
Secondary outcomes form a single Benjamini-Hochberg family and are listed in Section 3.5. The primary outcome is not a member of that family: it is tested once, without multiplicity adjustment, and is the only confirmatory test in the paper.

title: Amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day readmission after a heart failure hospitalization
text:
2.6 Covariates
Covariates were selected a priori on clinical grounds, not by stepwise selection or by a p-value screen. They fall into four blocks, entered sequentially in Section 3.4:

Demographic and administrative: age, sex, primary payer, ZIP-code income quartile, patient residence (NCHS urban-rural category), weekend admission, admission type, discharge year.
Hospital: bed size, urban-rural teaching status, ownership.
Comorbidity: the 31 Elixhauser comorbidity flags and the Elixhauser count. The alcohol-abuse and drug-abuse Elixhauser flags were excluded by pre-specification, because they are partly definitional of the exposure and including them would adjust away the exposure itself.
Clinical: heart failure phenotype, cardiogenic shock, cardiomyopathy, acute myocardial infarction at index, mechanical ventilation, chronic dialysis, cardiac implantable electronic device, tobacco dependence, housing instability.

Two modelling decisions deserve to be stated explicitly because reviewers ask about both.
Age is modelled as a restricted cubic spline (natural spline, 3 degrees of freedom), not as a linear term and not in categories. The relationship between age and readmission after heart failure is not linear, and categorizing a continuous covariate discards information and creates artefactual steps at the cut points. The exposed and unexposed arms differ substantially in age, so residual confounding by age is exactly the criticism this model must be able to withstand.
Chronic dialysis excludes ICD-10-PCS 5A1D90Z. That code denotes continuous renal replacement therapy in the setting of acute kidney injury, not maintenance dialysis, and including it would misclassify acutely ill patients as having end-stage renal disease.
Housing instability (Z59.x) is included as a covariate, and the model is also refitted without it (Section 3.3.2). It is strongly associated with both stimulant use and readmission, but it is captured by a Z code whose recording is incomplete and varies by hospital. Presenting the estimate with and without it shows the reader how much of the association it accounts for, rather than leaving that to speculation.
Length of stay, discharge disposition and discharge against medical advice are NOT adjusted for in the primary model. They lie on the causal pathway from stimulant use to readmission, and conditioning on them would remove part of the very association being estimated. They are entered only in Model 5 of the sequential series, which is labelled over-adjusted, showing mediation and must never be reported as the adjusted result.
Costs were obtained by applying HCUP cost-to-charge ratios to total charges and inflating to 2022 dollars using the Consumer Price Index. The series used is CPI-U, All Items, U.S. city average, not seasonally adjusted, annual average (CUUR0000SA0); see ?@sec-cpi-note.

2.7 Missing data
Categorical covariates with a defensible missing category (payer, ZIP income quartile, patient residence) retain an explicit “Missing/other” level rather than being dropped, so that no observation is lost and the amount of missingness is visible in Table 1. Continuous covariates and variables with no defensible missing category are complete-cased. The number of records removed by complete-casing is reported as the final step of Section 2.3. Multiple imputation was not used: missingness on the primary-model covariates is minimal and is not plausibly outcome-dependent, so imputation would add machinery without changing the estimate.

title: Amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day readmission after a heart failure hospitalization
text:
2.8 Statistical analysis

2.8.1 Primary model
The primary model is a survey-weighted logistic regression of 30-day all-cause readmission on amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder, adjusted for the covariate blocks above, fitted with survey::svyglm() and a quasibinomial family.
A Cox model is not the primary specification. Every patient has a fixed 30-day observation window and complete follow-up by design; there is no censoring other than the administrative censoring that applies identically to everyone. A Cox model is reported as sensitivity analysis S4, fitted on the full cohort with administrative censoring at day 30.


2.8.2 Absolute effects, by marginal standardization
Because 30-day readmission after heart failure is common, an odds ratio is a poor approximation to a risk ratio and overstates it. The headline effect measures are therefore absolute: adjusted risks in each arm, the adjusted risk difference and the adjusted risk ratio, obtained by marginal standardization (g-computation) over the observed covariate distribution of the whole cohort, with delta-method variance on the design degrees of freedom.
These are not predicted probabilities at covariate means, which would describe a patient who does not exist. They are the average risk that would be observed if the entire cohort were exposed, and if the entire cohort were unexposed.
The delta-method implementation was validated numerically before use, and each render re-verifies it against an independent implementation (marginaleffects::avg_comparisons()); the comparison is printed in Section 3.3.3 and a disagreement beyond the pre-specified tolerance stops the analysis.


2.8.3 Overlap weighting as a co-estimator
A propensity-score overlap-weighted (ATO) estimate is reported alongside the regression, never instead of it. Overlap weighting was preferred to matching and to inverse-probability weighting because it achieves exact balance on every covariate in the propensity model, has bounded weights (so there is no trimming rule to justify), and has the smallest variance among balancing weights. The outcome model is refitted on the overlap-weighted design, making the estimator doubly robust. The design-based variance treats the estimated weights as fixed, which is standard and mildly conservative for ATO.


2.8.4 Baseline comparison
Table 1 reports standardized mean differences, not p-values. With a cohort of this size every clinically trivial difference is statistically significant, so a p-value in Table 1 conveys sample size rather than imbalance. An absolute standardized mean difference below 0.10 is conventionally taken as balance.


2.8.5 Effect modification
Four subgroups were pre-specified: age under 55 versus 55 and over, HFrEF versus HFpEF, Medicaid versus other payer, and metropolitan versus non-metropolitan residence. All subgroup results are exploratory, are not multiplicity-adjusted, and do not appear in the Conclusions. Effect modification is assessed by a design-based Wald test on the whole interaction block, never by inspecting whether subgroup confidence intervals overlap. When the modifier is a deterministic collapse of a covariate already in the model (payer group of primary payer, residence group of NCHS category, phenotype of the phenotype variable), that covariate is removed from the interaction model so that no coefficient is aliased.
No sex subgroup was analysed: the exposed arm is heavily male, and such a test would be underpowered and uninformative.


2.8.6 Unmeasured confounding
An E-value is reported on the risk ratio scale – never on the odds ratio, which would overstate it. The E-value is the minimum strength of association, on the risk ratio scale, that an unmeasured confounder would need with both exposure and outcome, above and beyond the measured covariates, to explain away the observed association.


2.8.7 Negative control outcome
A negative control outcome – 30-day readmission with an eye or ear principal diagnosis – was pre-specified. Such a readmission has no plausible causal link to stimulant use. A null result is consistent with the absence of gross residual confounding or differential surveillance; a non-null result indicates one or the other and is reported as such.


2.8.8 Multiplicity
The primary outcome is tested once and is not adjusted. Secondary outcomes form one Benjamini-Hochberg family. Between-arm differences in cause of readmission form a second, separate Benjamini-Hochberg family. Subgroup and sensitivity analyses are not adjusted and are labelled exploratory or confirmatory-consistency respectively.

2.9 Small-cell suppression
Under the HCUP Data Use Agreement, no cell derived from fewer than 11 unweighted observations may be reported. Every rendered table is scanned programmatically at the end of the render (Section 7.1); suppressed cells appear as <11. Suppression is applied to figures as well as tables, so that no suppressed count can be recovered from a plotted value.

2.10 Software
Analyses were performed in R 4.6.1 using survey 4.5, survival 3.8.6, splines (base) and dplyr 1.2.1. Comorbidities were classified with the AHRQ Elixhauser Comorbidity Software and causes of readmission with the AHRQ Clinical Classifications Software Refined (DXCCSR v2025.1). This report was produced with Quarto; all tables and figures are generated from the analysis file at render time and none are transcribed by hand.

The following pre-specified covariates were removed by the sparse-cell guard because their smallest outcome cell fell below 11 unweighted discharges, which would otherwise cause quasi-complete separation: elix_chf. The Elixhauser drug-abuse and alcohol-abuse flags were excluded by pre-specification, not after inspection, because they are collinear with the exposure by construction. Nicotine dependence was deliberately not adjusted for: it is a near-universal co-code in the exposed arm and conditioning on it would be over-adjustment on a proxy of the exposure. Sequential Models 1 to 4 are NOT monotone – check whether a covariate has been misclassified as a mediator. The Model 4 to Model 5 change is attenuation consistent with mediation and is not an adjusted estimate.



3.3.1 Unmeasured confounding
An unmeasured confounder would need to be associated with both amphetamine-type stimulant use disorder and 30-day readmission by a risk ratio of at least 1.80 each, above and beyond the measured covariates, to explain away the observed adjusted risk ratio of 1.25; to move the confidence limit closest to the null to 1.00 the required association is 1.76. The most plausible such confounder here is housing instability, which is partly but not completely captured by the Z59.x diagnosis code included in the model.
